clue.text: Old person, carelessly lax inside, snuffed out taper

indicators.note: something done carelessly is jumbled, so the letters of the word beside it may be in any order
a flame that is snuffed out is extinguished, so those letters vanish from the longer word

parts.note: a wax light is a thin candle, a taper
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A careless old fellow lets a candle go out.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumbled, lax becomes the A, X and L found inside WAX LIGHT; snuff them out and WIGHT is left. 'Inside' says where those letters sit.
explanation.definitionFit: Wight is an archaic word for a human being or creature, used of an old fellow in older literature.

clue.text: Scottish angler put off by a big dew

indicators.note: something put off is disturbed or upset, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered

explanation.surface: A Scottish fisherman is deterred by a heavy morning dew.
explanation.walkthrough: The angler is not a fisherman but a fish, the monkfish-like angler with its huge mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Widegab is a Scots name for the anglerfish, named from its enormous gaping mouth.

clue.text: Fish bearing live young? You'll find us in African country

indicators.note: the pronoun is found in, inside the country name

parts.note: Gambia, or The Gambia, in West Africa
taken as written

explanation.surface: A live-bearing fish speaks up from its home in West Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Gambusia is the mosquitofish genus, small fish that give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.

clue.text: Spread by the sound of it what's often attached to loom

indicators.note: judged by its sound means the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to air views is to spread them

explanation.surface: A weaver's question about what is spread over the frame.
explanation.walkthrough: The loom is no weaving frame; the answer precedes it in the compound heirloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Heir is the first half of heirloom, the word most often joined to the front of loom.

clue.text: Type of rabbit — what might that be in Pacific tree?

indicators.note: the phrase sits in, within the name of the tree

parts.note: the ti is a palm-like Pacific tree
a rabbit might well be a pet

explanation.surface: A question about a rabbit sitting up in a Pacific tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' points back to the rabbit, which might be a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: The tapeti is the Brazilian rabbit, a wild cottontail of South and Central America.

clue.text: I'm a sadhu, endlessly transported in yogic meditation

indicators.note: being transported, carried off elsewhere, moves the letters into a new order
without its end, the holy man's title loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: A Hindu holy man describes being carried away in deep meditation.
explanation.walkthrough: A sadhu is a Hindu holy man; drop his last letter and rearrange with I'M A.
explanation.definitionFit: Samadhi is the state of deep absorbed concentration that is the goal of yoga practice in Hindu and Buddhist traditions.

clue.text: Winter driving hazard currently skirted by chauffeur

indicators.note: something skirted is edged all round, so the driver word encloses the time word

parts.note: a sice or syce is an Indian groom or driver
currently means at present

explanation.surface: A chauffeur steers round a dangerous patch on a winter road.
explanation.walkthrough: Sice is an Anglo-Indian word for a groom who also drives.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow-ice is ice formed from compacted or melted and refrozen snow, slippery on winter roads.

clue.text: Stray bit of garlic found in soy-based paste

indicators.note: found in places that letter inside the paste word

parts.note: miso is a Japanese fermented soybean paste

indicators.note: a bit of means just one small piece, the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of garlic

explanation.surface: A stray bit of garlic turns up in the miso.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' looks like an adjective for the garlic, but it is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To misgo is an old verb meaning to go astray or take the wrong path.

clue.text: Jig-like dancing on a mat round Italy

indicators.note: round means placed around, enclosing the country letter
letters that are dancing move about and change places

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: Someone dances an Italian jig on a mat.
explanation.definitionFit: Animato is a musical direction meaning lively and animated, as a jig is.

clue.text: Therapeutic exercise, such as Catch-22?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a system of deep bodywork and movement
second meaning: a book by the American novelist who wrote that satire

explanation.walkthrough: Catch-22 is Joseph Heller's 1961 war novel, so it is a Heller work.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellerwork is a structural bodywork therapy developed by Joseph Heller, a different man from the novelist.

clue.text: First player is on my left? Perfect

definitions.text: First player is on my left
definitions.meaning: first meaning, split in two: ..., since the player on the dealer's left leads
second meaning: flawless, as good as can be

explanation.walkthrough: In bridge and most card games play goes clockwise, so the first card is led by the player to the dealer's left.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal as an adjective describes something exactly as it should be, without fault.

clue.text: Whortleberry, source of an idea when opening grapery (10, two words)

indicators.note: the phrase is only the raw material the first word is made from, so its letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered
a grapery is where grapes grow, loosely the vine itself

explanation.surface: A berry is credited with sparking an idea at the opening of a vineyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The blogger was unsure of this one; the likeliest reading is the rearranged phrase opening, placed first, before the grapery word.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaean vine, the vine of Mount Ida, is an old name for the cowberry or red whortleberry shrub.

clue.text: Freshwater fish? Not what angler displays!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a black bass of North American rivers and lakes
second meaning, read literally: the angler fish has a huge gape, so a little one is not what it shows

explanation.walkthrough: The angler sounds like a fisherman, but it is the anglerfish, whose mouth is huge.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallmouth is a North American black bass found in clear rivers and lakes.

clue.text: Greek character, see, in boom making lolly

indicators.note: the letter and the sound are put in the middle of the spar word, enclosed by it

parts.note: a boom is a long spar or pole
a letter of the Greek alphabet
the letter C sounds like see

explanation.surface: A Greek seeing a boom being made into an ice lolly.
explanation.walkthrough: A lolly here is a British ice lolly, frozen flavoured water on a stick, which Americans call a Popsicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Popsicle is the trade name used in North America for an ice lolly on a stick.

clue.text: Beverage imbibed by uncle in the past, the old soak

indicators.note: a drink imbibed by someone ends up inside them, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: eme is an old word for an uncle
a brew is a drink

explanation.surface: An uncle of old is a drunkard who downs a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old soak' reads as a drunkard, but soak is a verb here and 'the old' warns that the word is archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Embrewe is a Spenserian form of imbrue, meaning to steep or drench in liquid.

clue.text: Fish end of tooth broken off

indicators.note: end of points at the final letter as the piece that goes
a piece that is broken off is lost, here the final letter of the grinding tooth

parts.note: a molar is a back grinding tooth

explanation.surface: A chipped tooth, as if bitten by a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' points at the last letter as the part that breaks away.
explanation.definitionFit: The mola is the ocean sunfish, a huge round-bodied marine fish.

clue.text: 3-part area, tons in brick-earth

parts.note: Caesar wrote that all Gaul is divided into three parts
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Tons of material spread across a three-part plot of clay ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gallic Wars opens 'Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres', so Gaul is the classic three-part area.
explanation.definitionFit: Gault is a stiff clay used for making bricks, which is just what brick-earth means.

clue.text: Riverside inn serving little over in varied table

indicators.note: the short letter goes in, enclosed by the reordered furniture word
something varied is changed about, so the letters of the furniture word are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered
a little over is its abbreviation, as on a cricket scoresheet

explanation.surface: A waterside pub serves small portions on a mixed table.
explanation.definitionFit: A boatel is a waterside hotel catering for people travelling by boat, blending boat and hotel.

clue.text: Unusual goat-trap displaying detachable cover (8, two words)

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are not in their usual order

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered

explanation.surface: An odd device for catching goats has a removable lid.
explanation.definitionFit: A targa top is a removable roof panel on a sports car, leaving the rear window fixed.

clue.text: Taking gee out flexed legs round old track, i.e. part them wide

indicators.note: round means wrapped around the track word
limbs that are flexed are bent into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged
gee is how the letter G is spelt, and taking it out removes it

parts.note: taken as written, then cut and reordered
trod is an old word for a path or track

explanation.surface: Instructions for a gymnast: bend the legs and open them wide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' refers back to the legs, so the definition borrows the wordplay's subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Strodle is an old form of straddle, to stand or sit with the legs spread wide apart.

clue.text: Apple sauce? Nothing replaces second ingredient

indicators.note: one letter replaces another, the second item in the sauce word, swapping it out

parts.note: custard is a sweet pouring sauce
nothing is zero, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A recipe for apple sauce with one ingredient swapped for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple sauce' reads as one dish, but Apple is the definition and sauce the wordplay; the U of CUSTARD becomes O.
explanation.definitionFit: Costard is an old English variety of large cooking apple, the source of the word costermonger.

clue.text: Tidy

parts.note: the bare definition of the competition word
in a plain competition puzzle solvers write this clue themselves, so only a definition is printed

explanation.walkthrough: This was the competition word: Azed gives only a definition, and entrants submit their own cryptic clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly describes things kept neat and in their proper places, arranged with method.

clue.text: Busy, in brief, sent abroad, we'll regulate strikes

indicators.note: in brief means shortened, so the slang word keeps only its opening

parts.note: busy is slang for a detective

indicators.note: abroad here means widely scattered, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered

explanation.surface: A busy official sent overseas promises to keep strikes under control.
explanation.walkthrough: The strikes are a clock's chimes, not industrial action; the answer speaks as 'we'.
explanation.definitionFit: Detents are catches in a clock's mechanism that control when and how often it strikes.

clue.text: Chip left in beer

indicators.note: the short letter is put in, inside the drink word

parts.note: bitter is a British style of beer
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A chip left floating in a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a hoppy British draught ale.
explanation.definitionFit: A blitter is a computer chip that moves blocks of graphics data in memory, a bit-blitter.

clue.text: Distant source of radiation in the capacity of timeless heavenly body

indicators.note: timeless means without the letter abbreviating time

parts.note: qua means in the capacity of
a star is a heavenly body

explanation.surface: A distant radiating object, acting as an eternal celestial body.
explanation.definitionFit: A quasar is an extremely remote active galactic nucleus emitting enormous radio and light energy.

clue.text: Clever clogs? One often goes with pants or boots

definitions.text: One often goes with pants or boots
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a word that commonly combines with pants or boots in compounds

explanation.walkthrough: Clogs, pants and boots make it all footwear and clothing, but the second half points at the compounds smartypants and smarty-boots. Clever clogs is British slang for a know-all.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarty is an informal word for a show-off who parades knowledge, the same person as a clever clogs.

clue.text: Canal boats are chastening with steamer around

indicators.note: the vessel abbreviation goes around, its two letters on either side

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
to cow is to subdue or chasten

explanation.surface: Barges are humbled when a steamship passes nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: Scows are flat-bottomed boats used for carrying cargo on canals and rivers.

clue.text: The N. English thoroughfare? A path of yesteryear

parts.note: in Northern English speech the is cut to t'
a road is a thoroughfare

explanation.surface: A Yorkshireman points out an old path.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern English dialect shortens the to t', as in 'down t' road'.
explanation.definitionFit: Troad is an obsolete Spenserian form of trode, meaning a path, track or course.

clue.text: Obscure tongue (not English) disowned

indicators.note: obscure means confused or unclear, so the letters are muddled
not English means the letter abbreviating English is removed from the word

parts.note: taken as written, then cut and reordered

explanation.surface: An obscure language, not English, that has been abandoned by its speakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ungot, an old form of ungotten, means not begotten, and so not acknowledged as one's own child.

clue.text: Salmon in group with similar character? Not right

indicators.note: not means the letters for the following word are taken away

parts.note: a cohort is a group sharing some common feature
RT is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A salmon swimming in a shoal of like fish, heading the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: Coho is a Pacific salmon species, also called the silver salmon, found off North America.

clue.text: Marine gastropod that's surprising when it's dry outside (7, two words)

indicators.note: the dry word stays outside, wrapping round the exclamation

parts.note: sere means dried up or withered
an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A sea creature that is a surprise to find on dry land.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea hare is a large sea slug, a mollusc whose head tentacles resemble a hare's ears.

clue.text: Hot oil carrier or tramp

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on a tap
an OBO is an ore, bulk and oil carrier ship

explanation.surface: A tanker, or a homeless wanderer, gets a mention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like the tramp steamer, keeping the ship theme, but it is a vagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobo is a homeless itinerant who wanders from place to place, a vagrant.

clue.text: Formerly abroad, we Scots will settle in Stroud strangely

indicators.note: settlers move in among the residents, so these letters go inside the town letters
arranged strangely means in an unusual order, so the town's letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written, then reordered
oo is a Scots form of we

explanation.surface: Scottish emigrants plan to make a new home in a Gloucestershire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Stroud is a town in Gloucestershire. Abroad's old sense is out of doors, out of the house.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English abroad meant out in the open air, beyond the house, the same as the modern adverb.

clue.text: Trouble in evidence of overweight, hence thresh around (10, two words)

indicators.note: the trouble word goes in, inside the phrase about the belly

parts.note: flab out, a paunch on show, is evidence of being too heavy
to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: An overweight person's trouble makes them thrash about.
explanation.walkthrough: The trouble word goes after the first two letters, splitting FLAB.
explanation.definitionFit: To thresh around is to thrash, moving the limbs wildly, which is exactly what flail about means.

clue.text: Toss around rubbish in scraps

indicators.note: the throwing word goes around, enclosing the rubbish word

parts.note: to shy is to throw
redd is a Scots and dialect word for rubbish or clearings

explanation.surface: Someone throws litter about, leaving it in bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Shreddy is a dialect adjective for torn into shreds or ragged, as anything left in scraps would be.

clue.text: Climbing parties? Knowledge of them indicates familiarity with procedure

definitions.meaning: first meaning, cryptically: the cords that tie a mountaineering team together, so they are party to the climb

definitions.text: Knowledge of them indicates familiarity with procedure
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the things you know when you know how a job is done, in the idiom

explanation.walkthrough: To know the ropes is an idiom for knowing how things work; climbers' cords supply the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbers are tied together by cords, and roped parties are teams linked that way on a mountain.
